title: The deploy script grants itself phUSD mint authority and never revokes it, while correctly revoking PhlimboV2's grant in the same run

description: `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, true)` is granted at `:1784`, `:2025` and `:2122` and is never revoked. Verified live at the end of the run: `phUSD.authorizedMinters(0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266) == (true, 1)`. The grant is a legitimate local shortcut — the deployer acts as a synthetic donor to seed the phUSD nudge stream, which story 073 sanctions — and the token is a mock on a chain whose keys are public, so there is no local risk. The finding is the inconsistency and what it costs the rehearsal: the SAME script, in the SAME run, correctly revokes PhlimboV2's grant as an explicit ordered step of the Phase 7.4 wind-down (verified: `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV2) == (false, 1)`, `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV3) == (true, 1)`), and logs it as such. So privilege revocation is clearly understood as a first-class cutover step here — just not applied to the deployer's own grant. Consequently the local chain's end state carries a live minter that mainnet's end state must not, and the 'revoke the operational key's temporary grant' step is never rehearsed even though it is precisely the kind of step that is easy to forget on a Ledger broadcast.
impact: No local risk (mock token, public anvil key). The cost is rehearsal fidelity: a residual-privilege sweep is never exercised, and the local end state differs from the intended mainnet end state in a way no assertion catches. This is an owner footgun of the non-obvious kind — the script's own careful revocation of the OTHER grant makes it read as though residual privileges were swept.
attackPath: NONE. No attacker is involved in any of the five findings at this entry point; `dev` is an anvil-only script that is never broadcast. C4 requires an attack path only for High/Medium, and no finding here is graded above Low.
recommendation: Revoke the deployer's grant at the end of `run()` with `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, false)` and assert it, mirroring the Phase 7.4 wind-down's own pattern. Better still, add a terminal 'residual privilege sweep' phase that asserts the full expected end-state ACL — deployer not a minter, PhlimboV2 not a minter, PhlimboV3 a minter — so the check is declarative and a future grant that forgets to clean up fails the run.
recommendationProvenance: VERBATIM from sanitized-findings.json, byte-for-byte. Non-empty verified.
evidenceSummary: cast-live-state.log holds all three authorizedMinters reads taken at the end of the run: deployer 0xf39Fd6...2266 == (true,1) [never revoked], PhlimboV2 == (false,1) [revoked as an explicit Phase 7.4 step], PhlimboV3 == (true,1). The asymmetry that carries the finding is visible in one file.

classification.c4Definition: QA/Low — access-control end state / operational hazard. Considered for the Centralization (C-01) bucket and rejected: no protocol asset sits behind the residual key, so labelling it a centralization risk would misdescribe it.
classification.assetImpact: None. The grant is on a MOCK phUSD, on chain 31337, to anvil key #0 (0xf39Fd6...2266) whose private key is published in Foundry's own documentation. There is no path from this grant to the real phUSD: DeployMocks deploys its own mock token, so even a mis-targeted run could not grant against the live minter ACL.
classification.functionOrAvailabilityImpact: None. The cost is that the 'revoke the operational key's temporary grant' step - exactly the step easiest to forget on a Ledger broadcast - is never rehearsed, and no assertion would catch its omission.
impactChain: 1. phUSD.setMinter(deployer, true) at :1784, :2025, :2122; never revoked. Verified live: authorizedMinters(0xf39Fd6...2266)==(true,1).
2. The grant itself is a sanctioned local shortcut (story 073): the deployer acts as synthetic donor to seed the phUSD nudge stream.

3. THE FOOTGUN: the SAME script in the SAME run explicitly revokes PhlimboV2's grant as a logged, ordered step of the Phase 7.4 wind-down (verified: PhlimboV2==(false,1), PhlimboV3==(true,1)) while leaving its own grant live.

4. SURPRISE TEST MET: a competent, non-malicious operator reading that careful wind-down would reasonably conclude the ACL had been swept. The asymmetry is the evidence it was an oversight, not a decision.
5. Realised harm: local end state carries a live minter the intended mainnet end state must not, and the residual-privilege sweep is absent from the rehearsal. No value at risk anywhere.

classification.externalRequirements: For any real risk, the pattern would have to recur in a mainnet broadcast script against the real phUSD - not observed at e1db0f1.

classification.lawNotes: Law 3 footgun, in scope, reported with safe-config guidance at honest severity.
classification.whyNotMedium: Law 3 says a non-obvious footgun is classified by the impact it unlocks, up to High - so no automatic downgrade applies and the ceiling was genuinely tested. It unlocks nothing: mock token, published test key, local chain, and no reachable path to the real phUSD minter ACL. Inflating this to Medium would charge the finding for the mainnet mistake it merely fails to rehearse against, which is culpability, not impact. Low, at the bottom of the Low bucket by impact.
classification.whyNotSuppressed: Explicitly NOT filtered as a 'reckless admin mistake'. Law 3 trusts the owner for KNOWING actions only; the same-run revocation asymmetry is positive evidence this one was not knowing.

rationale: A genuine non-obvious owner footgun (Law 3, in scope), classified by the impact it actually unlocks - which on a mock token on a public-key anvil chain is nil. The value of the finding is the rehearsal-fidelity gap and the pattern flag, both of which are Low.
